title: Incidental social category information influences scene evaluation and memory across cultures.
abstract: Visual cognition in naturalistic settings is inherently social, yet much of what is known about social categorisation derives from tasks in which group membership is made explicitly relevant. The present study examined whether social category information influences visual evaluation and memory when it is incidental to the task and embedded within visual scenes, and whether these effects differ across cultures. Two hundred and thirty-one participants from East Asian (China), South Asian (India) and European (United Kingdom and Poland) cultural groups evaluated images depicting either ingroup or outgroup individuals, followed by an unexpected memory test. Racial attitudes and the quality and quantity of intergroup contact were also measured. Images depicting ingroup members were evaluated more positively and remembered more accurately than those depicting outgroup individuals. Memory for images containing outgroup (but not ingroup) individuals was selectively associated with perceived interest. Negative racial attitudes predicted less favourable evaluation of outgroup images, but only among participants reporting lower intergroup contact. There was no evidence that these effects were moderated by participant nationality. Together, these findings suggest that social category information can influence evaluation and memory even when it is task irrelevant, with effects shaped by racial attitudes and intergroup contact.
